Comair Safety

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Kulula and BA Domestic and Regional flights have been grounded. What does this mean for parent company, Comair?

Unique Selling Point:
On 10 Feb 2022 Kulula Boeing 7373-800 with 157 passengers on board, on route from Lanseria to CPT had to make an emergency landing at ORT after one of its engines failed.
On 20 February, BA6252, EL to JHB had to make an emergency landing at East London shortly after takeoff when landing gear failed to retract.
On 5 March MN451 Took off from Lanseria and had to make an emergency landing at ORT because of an engine related issue.
On 12 March, Comair’s air certificate was suspended for 24 hours as a precautionary measure — effectively grounding the fleet and about 40% of SA's commercial flight capacity has been removed.

Summary:
Comair Limited is the parent company of two local brands, kulula.com and British Airways Domestic and Regional. It's listed on the stock exchange and has been in operation for more than 65 years and is one of South Africa's longest running airlines.

On Saturday, 12 March all Kulula and British Airways flights were suspended and the airline was grounded over safety concerns. Following the initial suspension, Comair was quick to rectify one of the operational issues raised by the Civil Aviation Authority, hoping to resume flights by Sunday 13 March. However, "Comair failed to demonstrate during the initial 24-hour suspension period that its risk and safety management systems are capable of managing potential hazards.” They have since been grounded indefinitely.

This is the 3rd time since 2007 that Comair has been grounded due to safety concerns.




Further information:
Comair has been in business rescue since May 2020. At this time CEO Wrenelle Stander was pushed out, and Glenn Orsmond moved into the hot-seat. Along with 4 other investors, they injected R500m into the company and managed to secure an additional R600m in additional borrowing, and R800m in deferred debt.

But the travel bans that came with the Omnicron breakout caused further setbacks for the company and they needed to make up an additional R100m loss.

The company has been restructuring since January 2022.

According to SAA Technical, Comair has poor maintenance management. Some of the biggest impacts of poor maintenance operations are: Out-of-control maintenance costs and Lost revenue… problems that have been plaguing Comair for some time.

Unions Solidarity and Numsa have expressed concerns over workers’ safety. And workplace satisfaction is at an all-time low according to a recent employee survey.

Add to that the fact that fuel prices have increased by about 40% since December.

Since the grounding, people are furious about the lack of communication, especially from Kulula. “Kulula customers will receive a full credit to the value of their ticket deposited in their Travel Bank for future travel valid for a period of six months,” added Kulula. But people are saying NO. They want money. Many are not planning to travel again within six months and by the looks of the company’s finances, it might not be around in six months’ time. CEO Glenn Orsmond has been quoted in the media: “We have chartered two aircraft to assist vulnerable passengers and those who most urgently need to travel.”… but this is not nearly enough to help many stranded travellers.

In the meantime about 40% of the country’s aviation capacity has been removed, and the Kulula and British Airways brands have suffered, what many are saying, irreparable damage… Comair seems to be treating this as an insignificant admin error that will be cleared up soon, and since other airlines are struggling to accommodate the air travel load, they seem to be confident that they’ll be up in the air, flying again soon!



INTERVIEW POSSIBILITIES

- I have an aircraft engineer who will speak to us anonymously about safety issues. How maintenance works and what the Level 1 and 2 concerns mean… as well as “what does it mean when the landing gear of a plane is stuck” or an “engine fails”

- Numsa - personel safety concerns

- Civil Aviation Authority - problems they have highlighted and Comair’s lack of compliance.

- Guy Leitch, Aviation expert

- Passenger onboard the aircraft that had to make an emergency landing.

- Passenger impacted by grounding of Comair/Kulula

- SAA Technical - the company that provides maintenance to commercial aircraft in the country..

- And first prize will be Glenn Orsmond from Comair - but he is apparently avoiding the media… (wonder why)

Press Release:


For decades a trusted brand, airline operator, Comair, is going through a period of turbulence. Three emergency landings in one month and a series of other apparent glitches have raised passenger safety concerns and earned the wrath of the Civil Aviation Authority. Could customer jitters and a precarious financial position bring the end of the runway into premature sight?
Carte Blanche takes a deeper look into what led to its crippling grounding.

Script:


Comair Collapse SCRIPT FINAL


Visuals Passengers praying
On-Screen 19 March 2022
V/O
Prayers onboard British Airways flight 6252 from East London to Cape Town. After takeoff the plane’s landing gear malfunctions and doesn't fully retract… the pilot makes an emergency landing.

One month later, BA flight 6324 experiences a technical glitch. It circles Cape Town airport twice to get visual confirmation that its landing gear is deployed, before touching down after circling for a 3rd time. It’s reported as a faulty cockpit warning light - normally, nothing to worry about.
V/O
But, as routine as this latest incident may have been, it couldn’t have come at a worse time for the plane’s operator, Comair Limited. A company with an exemplary historical safety and operational record, it’s had a troubled two weeks. So troubling in fact that some are asking: is Comair nearing the end of its runway?
LINK
This was a very different scene two weeks ago… Saturday the 12 of March, people made their way to airports across the country only to be met with closed gates and empty check-in counters…
V/O
News of Comair’s grounding travelled fast and within a few hours all the seats on competing airlines were sold out. Heading home to George that Sunday afternoon, Maranda van Dam was one of the lucky ones able to get a flight…
Maranda
It’s cost me close to 3000 grand. And I arrived safely, finally at six that evening
V/O
Except for a few social media posts, communication from Comair was … limited… and still is.
Even our requests for an interview were rejected.
Maranda
The Kulula helpdesk was closed. The blinds were closed. There was not a Kulula staff member anywhere in sight.
V/O
The Civil Aviation Authority‘s suspension of Comair’s Air Operator Certificate didn’t come out of the blue. It followed a series of incidents involving Kulula and British Airways over the past six weeks….

10 February - an in-flight engine shut down

Ten days later - landing gear fails to retract

And on 7 March - another engine related issue…
Donna Verrydt
Suddenly there was a very loud clang sound that came from the left engine. It was clear that something was very wrong.
V/O
Donna Verrydt was onboard the Kulula flight in February…
Donna Verrydt
Everybody was very scared. There were people who were trying to make contact with their families on the ground…
V/O
The CAA found weaknesses in Comair’s management systems. When an aircraft’s engine fails, for example, it’s not enough to simply replace the engine. Simon Segwabe is Executive for Aviation Safety Operations.
Simon Segwabe
You need to identify that risk with that specific operation so that you know, or you got a certain level of comfort the very same occurrence will not occur on the second one…
Guy Leitch
At the end of the day, it's actually administration which keeps airlines safe. It’s all about compliance. It's all about meeting all the extremely onerous terms and conditions of your aircraft operator's certificate…


V/o
Dr Guy Leitch has a PHD in African Aviation Connectivity and is the editor and publisher of SA Flyer magazine. While applauding the CAA for maintaining a high compliance standard, he’s not always convinced of their methods.
Dr Guy Leitch
00:06:09:12 - 00:06:57:08
Our own CAA is far too trigger happy. I don't know any other airline regulator anywhere in the world, which is as heavy handed as our own CAA is in terms of grounding airlines.


Simon Segwabe
00:02:54:22 - 00:03:28:27
We don't actually intend to appear to ground or suspend any operator. It is for that reason. When we find a deficiency in the system, we offer them the opportunity to address the deficiency. Only when they fail to do such is unfortunately the only option that we have is to protect the public by suspending operations.
V/o
The grounding of Comair Limited came at a very bad time for the company… adding to the embattled operator’s existing troubles.
LINK
When Covid hit in 2020 airlines across the world found themselves in financial trouble, and it was no different for Comair. In May that year the company went into voluntary business rescue…
Guy Leitch
Unfortunately, shortly before COVID, the airline went into a really strongly, shall we say, ambitious growth expansion phase, and it got a bit overextended. So it was very vulnerable when COVID hit.


V/O
After finding itself in the red for the first time in over 60 years of operation… a group of investors jumped in to save Comair Limited and its airlines, embarking on a rigorous cost-cutting exercise…
Simon Segwabe
I think they used to have a staff complement of 2200. They are now down to 1200. So that alone tells you there's been a significant change that requires constant, constant monitoring. And we could not find what how they’ve been managing the changes implemented following the restructuring.
Guy Leitch
There is talk that there's been a loss of skills and resources in Comair’s Safety Management Department, compliance department.
V/o
It is estimated that Comair Limited lost an additional R100 million at the end of last year due to the strict Covid Omicron travel bans…
Phakamile
Multiple retrenchment processes, salary cuts, cuts of benefits and conditions – all of these things have taken place at Comair in the last 2-3 years in the name of saving the airline.
V/O
Phakamile Hlubi-Mojola speaks for the National Union of Metalworkers. She says Comair’s cost-cutting has also cut the time that planes spend on the ground undergoing maintenance.
Phakamile
We know that because our members have actually raised this in various meetings with management. The technicians have repeatedly been recording in the logbook that they don’t have enough time to deal with certain issues in the time allocated.
V/O
But most of Comair’s aircraft maintenance is carried out by three independent companies - Lufthansa Technik, SAA Technical and Nevergreen. … All three of these maintenance organisations are now also under investigation by the CAA.
In a surprise move last week Comair cut ties with Lufthansa Technik, a German company with a solid international reputation.
Simon Segwabe
We have had the report for Lufthansa Technik. Yes there are deficiencies.
V/O
Not long after, the CAA suspended Lufthansa Technik’s approval, saying the company isn’t properly implementing management systems as set out in the CAA manuals.
But the reality is that the buck stops with Comair and its CEO – Glenn Orsmond - appointed in 2020. Ultimately, he’s responsible, no matter who does the maintenance.
UPSOUND
Glenn must go!
Guy Leitch
00:14:17:02 - 00:14:23:09
Union CEO Glen Osmond must resign. Is this fair? Should he go?

00:14:24:18 - 00:15:00:16
No, I think it's a knee jerk reaction. I think that skilled airline CEOs are very few and far between in South Africa. And Glenn Orsmond is undoubtedly one of the very best.
Phakamile
If this was a pilot who was responsible for the grounding of an airline, we wouldn’t be debating the removal of that pilot. But because we’re talking about a white CEO of a privately owned entity we are now debating that? This man has taken very direct decisions, in our view, that have led us to the point where we are right now. And if the board is serious about the steps that are necessary to enfuse confidence in the public’s mind, that indeed they are tackling issues to remedy the situation then the very first thing they need to do is replace Glenn with somebody who knows what he’s doing.
V/O
Although the grounding only lasted 5 days, the damage was done… and a lot of it.. by Comair itself…
LINK
The biggest frustration for many Kulula and BA passengers was the lack of communication from the airlines and Comair Limited. They wanted answers, but were not getting any…
Carmen Murray
We need to understand that every decision being made right now is going to impact Comair in the future. What you do now is what matters. And it's about listening to the voice of the customers.
V/O
Carmen Murray is a marketing expert and netnographer, using internet search data and social listening to guide companies…
Carmen Murray
All you need to do is go to your social media channels and you can see what people are saying. They are saying that where is the frontline staff? Nobody's there, but where is the leadership? And one of the most damaging things for organizations is when the leadership is not present.

Guy Leitch
I don't think that Comair did a good job on communications at all. Again, one could blame cost cutting that they tend to to cut down on this hopefully not immediate staff. But most of the passengers were extremely irate that they were kept in the dark…
V/O
And not surprisingly, people want to know: are their aeroplanes safe?
Carmen Murray
One of the biggest trends that we are seeing is the fact that there's been a massive increase in the search around flight safety.
Now that flight safety searches are not just pertaining to Comair. And what's been created by one airline does not just impact one specific company, but the entire industry.
V/O
Whether Comair reclaims its place in the country’s aviation sector remains to be seen. Right now, the fall-out from their grounding is far from over…
Guy Leitch
One of the knock-on effects I fear from this is the loss of the British Airways franchise, because obviously British Airways itself may be worried about the reputational damage suffered by its own brand with this grounding…


_____










PROMO 1 11”
A spate of recent aircraft emergencies led to the grounding of Comair Limited’s fleet for 5 days. Is the cash-strapped operator cutting costs at the expense of safety?
PROMO 2 21”
Thousands of stranded air travellers, an airline operator in business rescue…
Phakamile: This airline’s cost-cutting measures are so drastic, that it’s had an impact on safety measures.
We investigate a recent spate of aircraft emergencies, and what that means for the future of the carriers.
UPSOUND DONNA: Our safety wasn’t their first priority and I will never take that chance again….


PROMO 3 21”
UPSOUND Phakamile: Multiple retrenchment processes, salary cuts…

Covid and financial troubles have led to the significant down-sizing of one of South Africa’s most successful airline operators…

UPSOUND SIMON: They used to have a staff complement of 2200. They’re now down to 1200.



Despite the odds stacked against it, can Comair soar once more?

It was clear that something was very wrong. V/O Donna Verrydt was onboard the Kulula flight in February… Donna Verrydt Everybody was very scared. There were people who were trying to make contact with their families on the ground… V/O The CAA found weaknesses in Comair’s management systems. When an aircraft’s engine fails, for example, it’s not enough to simply replace the engine. Simon Segwabe is Executive for Aviation Safety Operations. Simon Segwabe You need to identify that risk with that specific operation so that you know, or you got a certain level of comfort the very same occurrence will not occur on the second one… Guy Leitch At the end of the day, it's actually administration which keeps airlines safe. It’s all about compliance. It's all about meeting all the extremely onerous terms and conditions of your aircraft operator's certificate… V/o Dr Guy Leitch has a PHD in African Aviation Connectivity and is the editor and publisher of SA Flyer magazine. While applauding the CAA for maintaining a high compliance standard, he’s not always convinced of their methods. Dr Guy Leitch 00:06:09:12 - 00:06:57:08 Our own CAA is far too trigger happy. I don't know any other airline regulator anywhere in the world, which is as heavy handed as our own CAA is in terms of grounding airlines. Simon Segwabe 00:02:54:22 - 00:03:28:27 We don't actually intend to appear to ground or suspend any operator. It is for that reason. When we find a deficiency in the system, we offer them the opportunity to address the deficiency. Only when they fail to do such is unfortunately the only option that we have is to protect the public by suspending operations. V/o The grounding of Comair Limited came at a very bad time for the company… adding to the embattled operator’s existing troubles. LINK When Covid hit in 2020 airlines across the world found themselves in financial trouble, and it was no different for Comair. In May that year the company went into voluntary business rescue… Guy Leitch Unfortunately, shortly before COVID, the airline went into a really strongly, shall we say, ambitious growth expansion phase, and it got a bit overextended. So it was very vulnerable when COVID hit. V/O After finding itself in the red for the first time in over 60 years of operation… a group of investors jumped in to save Comair Limited and its airlines, embarking on a rigorous cost-cutting exercise… Simon Segwabe I think they used to have a staff complement of 2200. They are now down to 1200. So that alone tells you there's been a significant change that requires constant, constant monitoring. And we could not find what how they’ve been managing the changes implemented following the restructuring. Guy Leitch There is talk that there's been a loss of skills and resources in Comair’s Safety Management Department, compliance department. V/o It is estimated that Comair Limited lost an additional R100 million at the end of last year due to the strict Covid Omicron travel bans… Phakamile Multiple retrenchment processes, salary cuts, cuts of benefits and conditions – all of these things have taken place at Comair in the last 2-3 years in the name of saving the airline. V/O Phakamile Hlubi-Mojola speaks for the National Union of Metalworkers. She says Comair’s cost-cutting has also cut the time that planes spend on the ground undergoing maintenance. Phakamile We know that because our members have actually raised this in various meetings with management. The technicians have repeatedly been recording in the logbook that they don’t have enough time to deal with certain issues in the time allocated. V/O But most of Comair’s aircraft maintenance is carried out by three independent companies - Lufthansa Technik, SAA Technical and Nevergreen. … All three of these maintenance organisations are now also under investigation by the CAA. In a surprise move last week Comair cut ties with Lufthansa Technik, a German company with a solid international reputation. Simon Segwabe We have had the report for Lufthansa Technik. Yes there are deficiencies. V/O Not long after, the CAA suspended Lufthansa Technik’s approval, saying the company isn’t properly implementing management systems as set out in the CAA manuals. But the reality is that the buck stops with Comair and its CEO – Glenn Orsmond - appointed in 2020. Ultimately, he’s responsible, no matter who does the maintenance. UPSOUND Glenn must go! Guy Leitch 00:14:17:02 - 00:14:23:09 Union CEO Glen Osmond must resign. Is this fair? Should he go? 00:14:24:18 - 00:15:00:16 No, I think it's a knee jerk reaction. I think that skilled airline CEOs are very few and far between in South Africa. And Glenn Orsmond is undoubtedly one of the very best. Phakamile If this was a pilot who was responsible for the grounding of an airline, we wouldn’t be debating the removal of that pilot. But because we’re talking about a white CEO of a privately owned entity we are now debating that? This man has taken very direct decisions, in our view, that have led us to the point where we are right now. And if the board is serious about the steps that are necessary to enfuse confidence in the public’s mind, that indeed they are tackling issues to remedy the situation then the very first thing they need to do is replace Glenn with somebody who knows what he’s doing. V/O Although the grounding only lasted 5 days, the damage was done… and a lot of it.. by Comair itself… LINK The biggest frustration for many Kulula and BA passengers was the lack of communication from the airlines and Comair Limited. They wanted answers, but were not getting any… Carmen Murray We need to understand that every decision being made right now is going to impact Comair in the future. What you do now is what matters. And it's about listening to the voice of the customers. V/O Carmen Murray is a marketing expert and netnographer, using internet search data and social listening to guide companies… Carmen Murray All you need to do is go to your social media channels and you can see what people are saying. They are saying that where is the frontline staff? Nobody's there, but where is the leadership? And one of the most damaging things for organizations is when the leadership is not present. Guy Leitch I don't think that Comair did a good job on communications at all. Again, one could blame cost cutting that they tend to to cut down on this hopefully not immediate staff. But most of the passengers were extremely irate that they were kept in the dark… V/O And not surprisingly, people want to know: are their aeroplanes safe? Carmen Murray One of the biggest trends that we are seeing is the fact that there's been a massive increase in the search around flight safety. Now that flight safety searches are not just pertaining to Comair. And what's been created by one airline does not just impact one specific company, but the entire industry. V/O Whether Comair reclaims its place in the country’s aviation sector remains to be seen. Right now, the fall-out from their grounding is far from over… Guy Leitch One of the knock-on effects I fear from this is the loss of the British Airways franchise, because obviously British Airways itself may be worried about the reputational damage suffered by its own brand with this grounding… _____ PROMO 1 11” A spate of recent aircraft emergencies led to the grounding of Comair Limited’s fleet for 5 days. UPSOUND DONNA: Our safety wasn’t their first priority and I will never take that chance again…. PROMO 3 21” UPSOUND Phakamile: Multiple retrenchment processes, salary cuts… Covid and financial troubles have led to the significant down-sizing of one of South Africa’s most successful airline operators… UPSOUND SIMON: They used to have a staff complement of 2200. They’re now down to 1200. Despite the odds stacked against it, can Comair soar once more?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Kulula and BA Domestic and Regional flights have been grounded. What does this mean for parent company, Comair?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: On 10 Feb 2022 Kulula Boeing 7373-800 with 157 passengers on board, on route from Lanseria to CPT had to make an emergency landing at ORT after one of its engines failed. On 20 February, BA6252, EL to JHB had to make an emergency landing at East London shortly after takeoff when landing gear failed to retract. On 5 March MN451 Took off from Lanseria and had to make an emergency landing at ORT because of an engine related issue. On 12 March, Comair’s air certificate was suspended for 24 hours as a precautionary measure — effectively grounding the fleet and about 40% of SA's commercial flight capacity has been removed.
metadata.Summary: Comair Limited is the parent company of two local brands, kulula.com and British Airways Domestic and Regional. It's listed on the stock exchange and has been in operation for more than 65 years and is one of South Africa's longest running airlines. On Saturday, 12 March all Kulula and British Airways flights were suspended and the airline was grounded over safety concerns. Following the initial suspension, Comair was quick to rectify one of the operational issues raised by the Civil Aviation Authority, hoping to resume flights by Sunday 13 March. However, "Comair failed to demonstrate during the initial 24-hour suspension period that its risk and safety management systems are capable of managing potential hazards.” They have since been grounded indefinitely. This is the 3rd time since 2007 that Comair has been grounded due to safety concerns.
metadata.Further information: Comair has been in business rescue since May 2020. At this time CEO Wrenelle Stander was pushed out, and Glenn Orsmond moved into the hot-seat. Along with 4 other investors, they injected R500m into the company and managed to secure an additional R600m in additional borrowing, and R800m in deferred debt. But the travel bans that came with the Omnicron breakout caused further setbacks for the company and they needed to make up an additional R100m loss. The company has been restructuring since January 2022. According to SAA Technical, Comair has poor maintenance management. Some of the biggest impacts of poor maintenance operations are: Out-of-control maintenance costs and Lost revenue… problems that have been plaguing Comair for some time. Unions Solidarity and Numsa have expressed concerns over workers’ safety. And workplace satisfaction is at an all-time low according to a recent employee survey. Add to that the fact that fuel prices have increased by about 40% since December. Since the grounding, people are furious about the lack of communication, especially from Kulula. “Kulula customers will receive a full credit to the value of their ticket deposited in their Travel Bank for future travel valid for a period of six months,” added Kulula. But people are saying NO. They want money. Many are not planning to travel again within six months and by the looks of the company’s finances, it might not be around in six months’ time. CEO Glenn Orsmond has been quoted in the media: “We have chartered two aircraft to assist vulnerable passengers and those who most urgently need to travel.”… but this is not nearly enough to help many stranded travellers. In the meantime about 40% of the country’s aviation capacity has been removed, and the Kulula and British Airways brands have suffered, what many are saying, irreparable damage… Comair seems to be treating this as an insignificant admin error that will be cleared up soon, and since other airlines are struggling to accommodate the air travel load, they seem to be confident that they’ll be up in the air, flying again soon! INTERVIEW POSSIBILITIES - I have an aircraft engineer who will speak to us anonymously about safety issues. How maintenance works and what the Level 1 and 2 concerns mean… as well as “what does it mean when the landing gear of a plane is stuck” or an “engine fails” - Numsa - personel safety concerns - Civil Aviation Authority - problems they have highlighted and Comair’s lack of compliance. - Guy Leitch, Aviation expert - Passenger onboard the aircraft that had to make an emergency landing. - Passenger impacted by grounding of Comair/Kulula - SAA Technical - the company that provides maintenance to commercial aircraft in the country.. - And first prize will be Glenn Orsmond from Comair - but he is apparently avoiding the media… (wonder why)
